paper_title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layerstep pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layerstep Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), trainingfree sparsity allocation method. Treating each layerstep pair as cell, ALLOT estimates each cells contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings. 1. Introduction Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [17] have been widely adopted for video generation. Models such as Wan [19] and HunyuanVideo [11] produce high-quality, spatio-temporally consistent videos, yet the cost of their full 3D attention grows quadratically with the number of tokens [18]. On single GPU, Wan2.1-14B takes roughly one hour to generate 720p, 81-frame video, and attention accounts for more than half of the end-to-end time. Sparse attention has been widely studied as means of reducing this computational cost, with existing approaches broadly categorized as either training-free or training-based. *Work done during an internship at KlingAI. Corresponding author. Many training-free methods [14, 24, 25, 29] adopt blocksparse attention, which partitions query and key tokens into blocks. These methods estimate the importance of each querykey block pair and compute dense attention only for selected pairs. These works primarily address two questions: which blocks participate in the attention computation, and how to execute the resulting sparse computation efficiently at the kernel level. Notably, beyond determining which blocks participate in the computation, the number of blocks retained in each layer at each denoising step also significantly affects generation quality and latency. In threshold-based methods [14, 24, 29], the thresholds serve as an implicit allocation rule. With all other conditions identical, changing only the allocation can substantially alter final-video fidelity. Despite the existence of some explicit allocation approaches, existing methods generally have the following two limitations: Heuristic rules do not transfer reliably across settings. Many works use fixed rules, such as keeping the first layer or the first 1030% of denoising steps dense [12, 14, 25]. Our measurements in 3 show that effective allocations vary across models and selection strategies. Consequently, rule tuned for one setting does not reliably transfer to another and must be re-tuned. Local metrics do not capture final-video effects. Automatic allocation methods commonly rely on local proxies, such as cumulative attention mass [14, 24], Hellinger distance [36], and one-step output error [3, 35], rather than direct measurements of final-video error. Our analysis in 3 shows that the rankings induced by these proxies disagree with those based on final-video error, and allocations guided by these metrics can even yield lower final-video fidelity than uniform baseline. To address these limitations, we term each (layer, step) pair cell and evaluate it directly by its sensitivity, defined as the degradation it induces in the final video relative to the dense output. Building on this formulation, we propose Allocating Layerstep Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), training-free latency allocation method. ALLOT estimates each cells sensitivity from two factors: cell probing measures the error injected at its step, and traFigure 1. Changing only the allocation at equal wall-clock time. Left: dense, baseline and + ALLOT (top to bottom), with blue-box insets; prompts are near the median gain. Right: paired PSNR gains (ALLOT baseline) with 95% CIs for Tabs. 1 and 2; open markers denote ties. jectory calibration measures how subsequent denoising steps amplify or attenuate that error. It then jointly allocates all cell densities under measuredlatency budget, so warm-up length and dense layers emerge from the solution rather than hand-set rules. Because sensitivity rankings remain stable across inputs for fixed model and selection strategy (3), we perform both measurements once offline and reuse their results across prompts. During inference, ALLOT looks up densities in precomputed table and changes only the allocation in existing block-sparse attention pipelines. Overall, our main contributions are threefold: We show that final-video sensitivity varies by orders of magnitude across layers and steps and is misjudged by local metrics, while sensitivity rankings remain stable across inputs. We propose ALLOT, which estimates each cells error by combining one-step cell probe with trajectory gain and jointly solves for all cell densities under measuredlatency budget, replacing only the allocation of existing pipelines. Extensive experiments across six selection strategies and three model families show that ALLOT outperforms or ties every compared allocation at equal or shorter wall-clock time (5). 2. Related Work Block-sparse attention. Block-sparse attention methods for video DiTs are either trained or training-free. Trained methods (VSA [30], VMoBA [21], NABLA [15]) train or fine-tune the model with sparse attention. Training-free methods either apply static masks [12, 31, 36] or select blocks at run time [14, 2225, 29]. ALLOT retains the selection strategies and kernels of existing methods, replacing only the allocation (4.5). Allocation in existing methods. Existing methods allocate density, threshold or sparse pattern per layer [3], per (layer, head) [1, 14, 35], per step [9, 33], per (layer, step) [28], or per (step, layer, head) [27, 36], based on attention mass, Hellinger distance, one-step output error or other local metrics. Across steps, most use heuristic warm-up or preset shape, or treat all steps equally. ALLOT also allocates per (layer, step) but calibrates each cell against the final video to capture cross-step error amplification and solves for all cells jointly under measured-latency budget. 3. Motivation and Key Observations Setup. Let ℓ index layers and index denoising steps. The sensitivity S(ℓ, s; b) of cell (ℓ, s) measures how much sparsifying that cell to density degrades the final video relative to the dense reference. Measuring this directly for every cell would require thousands of full generations and is therefore impractical. We instead decompose it into two cheaper signals: the one-step output error when one layer is sparsified and the final-video error when window of steps is sparsified (4.2, 4.3). Observation 1: Layer sensitivity varies widely and is not reliably reflected by attention-map metrics. As shown in Figure 2(a), the first one or two layers have one-step errors up to 154 times the median-layer error. When evaluated on the final video, the most sensitive layers coincide with these higherror layers. Attention-map metrics (attention mass [14] and Hellinger distance [36]) yield different sensitivity rankings, and allocations based on them degrade fidelity (Appendix B). Cell probes therefore provide more reliable basis for layer allocation. The most sensitive layer varies across models, and fixed first layer dense rule therefore does not transfer reliably across settings. 2 Figure 2. Layer and step sensitivity. (a) Single-layer one-step error (b=0.30, t=0.85; bars), attention-map metrics [14, 36] (lines), and final-video MSE with that layer sparse throughout (diamonds). Titles give the most sensitive layer and its metric ranks. (b) Wan2.1-1.3B window errors versus local metrics [33]; annotations give first/last-window ratios. (c) Window errors across four models. Observation 2: Final-video effects vary sharply across denoising steps and are understated by one-step errors. As shown in Figure 2(b, c), earlier windows produce markedly larger final-video errors than later ones under the same sparsification configuration. The first-to-last-window MSE ratio reaches several hundred for some models. By contrast, the corresponding one-step errors show much smaller difference and even reverse the ordering of the first and last windows on Wan2.2. One-step errors therefore require trajectory calibration before guiding per-step density. Observation 3: Sensitivity rankings remain stable across inputs for fixed model and selection strategy. Across all tested models, per-input sensitivity rankings closely match rankings aggregated over calibration inputs, with median Spearman correlations of 0.801.00 (Appendix D). Prior work reports similar input stability for attention-map metrics [14, 36]. Our results extend this observation to outputerror sensitivity, allowing cell probes and trajectory gains to be measured offline and reused across prompts. 4. It consists of three modules: cell probing (4.2), trajectory calibration (4.3) and latencyconstrained allocation (4.4), built on the first-order analysis and calibrated estimate of 4.1. 4.5 describes inference and integration with existing pipelines. 4.1. The bisection locates the two Lagrangian tables bracketing C, which typically differ in only one cell (Appendix E). Warmup length, which layers stay dense and how density varies across steps all emerge from the solver without heuristic rules (Appendices and J). 5 4.5. Inference and integration with existing selection strategies Inference. The density table is solved offline, once per model, selection strategy and latency budget. At generation time, the density of each layer is set from the table before each step s. Cells with bℓs=1 use the original dense attention. All other cells are sparsified by the selection strategy at density bℓs and computed by the original kernel. The same table is used for all prompts. Changing the budget only requires re-solving one table. Integration. ALLOT keeps each selection strategys kernel and ranking, replacing only the cutoff that determines how many ranked blocks or clusters are retained. Thresholdbased defaults (SVOO, SVG2, SpargeAttn and XAttention) are converted to density cutoff. For SpargeAttn, this uses its official top-k API. This removes native per-head or per-input adaptation. Splitting by SVOOs head densities is 1.44 dB worse than an equal split (Appendices and F). Throughout, changing only the allocation refers to this integration. Supported interfaces. ALLOT applies when selection strategy supports controllable per-cell density and its latency can be measured. Fixed-mask strategies such as Radial are restricted to densities reachable by their mask parameters. Density denotes retained blocks for mean-pooled top-k, SpargeAttn, Radial and XAttention, and retained key tokens for the variable-size clusters of SVOO and SVG2. 5. Experiments 5.1. Experimental setup Models and data. Four models: Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and 14B (hereafter 1.3B and 14B), Wan2.2-T2V-A14B [19] and HunyuanVideo [11]. Resolution and frame count are given in each table, following published setting where one exists. The analyses in 3 use 480p33. All use 50 denoising steps. Wan2.2 results are in Tabs. 2 and 3, and HunyuanVideo results are in Tab. 2 and Appendices and J. The evaluation set consists of 32 VBench [10] prompts. Metrics. Fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM [20] and LPIPS [32]) measure similarity to the dense reference (same prompt and seed) rather than absolute generation quality. Perceptual quality is measured by VBench [10], weighted over the six dimensions used by HEART [35]. At matched or shorter wall-clock time, win requires positive lower bound of the paired 95% PSNR-difference interval and lower mean LPIPS, while loss requires negative upper bound and higher mean LPIPS. All other cases are ties, and VBench does not enter the verdict (Appendix A). Baselines. Published pipelines [12, 14, 24, 25, 29] follow their documented settings (SVG2 uses HEARTs five-step warm-up), while allocation baselines [3, 9, 27, 28, 33, 35, 36] are re-implemented from their papers (Appendices and H). For mean-pooled top-k, the uniform baseline keeps the first 15 steps dense. The strengthened baseline additionally keeps layer 0 dense and tunes the warm-up on 1.3B (Appendix J). Implementation details. Mean-pooled top-k (the coarse stage of VSA [30]) reorders tokens cube by cube (344 cubes) and groups every 64 consecutive tokens into block. Cell probes are measured on four OpenVid [16] real videos over grid of 8 densities 9 noise levels. Trajectory gains are measured using 10 five-step windows at window density b0=0.30. 5.2. Comparison with other allocation methods To compare allocation strategies in isolation, we fix XAttentions selection strategy and kernel, changing only the allocation (Tab. 1). ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation method, all of which use hand-set rules or local metrics, by 1.537.31 dB. The effect of density truncation depends on the selection strategy: it lowers SVOOs PSNR but improves XAttentions. ALLOT further improves on XAttentions density-cutoff default at matched wall-clock time (Appendix F). VBench scores remain close to those of the baselines. ALLOT also outperforms every compared allocation method on additional XAttention settings spanning higher resolution and HunyuanVideo, all at equal or shorter wall-clock time (Appendix G). 5.3. Integration with published pipelines We integrate ALLOT into the official pipelines of SVOO [14], SVG2 [25], SpargeAttn [29] and Radial [12], changing only the allocation (Tab. 2, details in Appendix H). ALLOT outperforms the default in six of the nine settings (by up to 5.03 dB in PSNR) and ties in the other three (Appendix H). Notably, on HunyuanVideo (13B) with SVOO, ALLOT improves PSNR by 3.38 dB while increasing endto-end speedup from 1.75 to 1.90. Figure 4 shows qualitative comparisons. To compare across speeds, we solve ALLOTs tables at several latency budgets on three published pipelines (1.3B 720p) and plot PSNR against end-to-end speedup (Figure 5). All of the pipelines own settings (open circles) lie below ALLOTs curve. 5.4. Cross-model comparison On the three Wan models with mean-pooled top-k, ALLOT outperforms both the uniform and the strengthened baseline (Tab. 3). We extend this comparison to HunyuanVideo at equal density in Appendix J. Figure 6 shows what fixed rule misses: the first few layers and certain deeper layers stay dense longest, while density decreases over several intermediate steps rather than dropping at single step. The best rule also changes with the budget, so we test the baselines at other budgets: ALLOT remains above the uniform baseline across budgets at 720p81 (1.3B and 14B, Appendix H). On 1.3B 480p33, it also outperforms the strengthened baseline with its warm-up re-searched at each of three budgets (Appendix J). 5.5. Ablation study Each ablation replaces one component in the XAttention setup of Tab. 1 at ALLOTs cost. Trajectory calibration is dominant: setting w(s) = 1 for every step lowers PSNR by 7.05 dB, and DiTFastAttns greedy rule on the same onestep errors reaches similar 19.38 dB (Tabs. 1 and 4). shared density across layers and parametric shape rule also underperform, whereas density-proportional cost makes no significant difference after wall-clock alignment. Meanpooled top-k ablations and an LPIPS-calibrated variant are reported in Appendix I. 5.6. Verification, robustness and offline cost Verifying the sensitivity estimate. The solver ranks density tables by their estimated total sensitivity, the sum of ˆS over all cells (Eq. (3)). We validate this ranking against measured final-video error. At fixed total cost, permuting ALLOTs densities among cells lowers PSNR on every prompt, and the measured ordering matches the prediction. Across 80 tables at multiple budgets on held-out prompts, the predicted and measured rankings agree strongly (pooled Kendall τ = 0.83, Appendix E). Number of calibration inputs. Cell probes use four probing videos and trajectory calibration uses eight prompts. With single probing video or calibration prompt, most cells keep the same dense/sparse status. On the XAttention setting of Tab. 1, eight probing videos bring no significant gain over four, and one or two lose less than tenth of ALLOTs gain (Appendix K). Window density and probe resolution have mild effects. Calibration with SpargeAttn rather than meanpooled top-k gives 0.993 correlation in and 96.096.5% cell-decision agreement (Appendix K). Offline cost. Measurement takes roughly 623 GPU-hours per model (over 30 for the two experts of Wan2.2) and is done once per model and selection strategy (Appendix F). Changing the latency budget or the number of steps only requires re-solving the table, which takes about 4 on CPU. With 30 steps, CFG 7.5 or the Euler sampler, ALLOT still outperforms the default without re-measuring (Appendix K). 6 Table 1. Verdicts. win requires the lower bound of the paired PSNR interval to be > 0 and the mean LPIPS to be lower; loss requires the upper bound of the PSNR interval to be < 0 and the mean LPIPS to be higher; everything else is tie. The appendix tables additionally list DISTS [4] as supplement only. Paired differences are ALLOT baseline, followed by the 95% t-interval over prompts and the numbers of prompts on which ALLOT is better/worse. Trajectory gain. The trajectory gain is calibrated once per model family (Wan2.1 on 1.3B 480p33 with meanpooled top-k, Wan2.2-A14B, and HunyuanVideo 480p33), and its window experiments are shared by all tables of that family across selection strategies, resolutions and model sizes. SVG2s official pipeline uses different flow shift, so its window experiments are rerun on that schedule. A.2.
